text_post: I got to be thinking about different lifestyles that can cause problems in relationships and one was the lifestyle of owning a dog or even pets in general.  A lot of people love dogs and see them as part of their family that a partner would potentially fit into eventually. I think it’s a massive lifestyle choice and difference between people that perhaps doesn’t get mentioned much. So my question is, would you date someone with a dog? Or if you have a dog, would it bother you if your partner was NOT a dog lover? For me I am not a pet person and the idea feels strange to me to share my home with animals, even though this is considered the social norm. I would not want to live with someone who has a dog although as far as pets go, I could handle a cat as I do really like cats even though I wouldn’t go out of my way to have one live with me as such. My preference is a pet free household.

author: oncebitten55
text_post: NORMAL, not exotic house cats are pretty easy to own and take care of. They are loners and don't require a ton of attention. Not all mind you, but most. If you want a good lap-cat, get a male cat. They tend to need and give you more attention then the females need, and are more loyal, but not like a dog "loyal". They will walk away when they are tired of anything, including being petted.  Indoor/outdoor cats are the best. Find a good huntress, get her fixed, and she will spend most of her time out hunting down game. ( in the cat world, female cats are as good, or better than males, when it comes to hunting and killing things) Domestic shorthairs don't shed much, but they do shed, but being outdoors a lot, you won't spend as much money on food and cat litter. The only downside is the vet bills if they get sick. And having to bury them when they die. Not fun at all. Keep them well hydrated as cats kidneys are a weaker part of their systems. Good clean water is cheaper then a cat with Feline Kidney Disease. I know this from personal experience, not hearsay. House cats are desert animals, so they will be inside more come winter. In summer, they will lay on the hot ground, bricks, concrete, ect, and it doesn't bother them at all. Oh, and a heterosexual guy having a cat for a pet? Anyone thinks I am gay can go "F" themselves. I like cats, period. I like how they can stay in one spot for hours if need be, to take out a mouse, rat, snakes or a bird. And you don't need to walk them either, like a dog or clean up their fecal matter, other then the kitty-box, since they cover their "tracks" by burying it. You can also be gone from home for a few days with no problems too. Cats can take care of themselves pretty well. Oh yeah, they don't bark either, although if you don't fix a female, she will make it well known that she is in heat. Fix her.

author: ukshygirl
text_post: I do love and respect seeing the bond many people have with their dogs as they are very loyal and often a companion people can rely on. However, my reasons for not feeling able to live with one are as follows. 1) I live frugally and I don't want the expense of trying to look after a dog or any pet.  2) I'd worry a partner with a dog would judge me for not feeling for their dog as much as they do and that it'd make for a disconnect for them if I don't connect with their pet as well as they do or many other women would. 3) I'm hyper sensitive in a way and I wouldn't want a dog jumping up on me or licking my face. It isn't comfortable for me.  4) I hate poop and would hate having to clear up over the dog generally when there's enough life tasks to deal with. I can't cope with the poop and mess.  5) Living with a dog would heighten my anxiety over it trashing stuff at home or impacting on other people. Living frugally means I don't want to have to replace my stuff or a neighbour's if he/she trashed theirs. I realise not all dogs do this but anxiety makes people see the worst. 6) I'd feel limited or tied down as I would want to take trips away with a partner sometimes and it's harder to do when you have pets.  A dog is overall a big lifestyle choice like having kids that two people need to be on the same page over, I think. I don't think dog owners are anymore entitled than anyone else but I do think there are entitled dog owners out there. I remember once I was sitting in an outdoor pub having a meal with my sister and a loose dog ran under our table and hovered, brushing against our feet. My sister was horrified and let out a gasp of "ahh" in horror and their reaction was "Wrong people". I do think that was an entitled and rude reaction, rather than just saying "Sorry about that" and calling the dog back to them.  Another time, I was at someone's house and acted anxious as their dog jumped up at me. They said,"You don't like dogs, do you?" I said how I just get nervous when he jumps up at me and they said "Well, it's his house". I wasn't complaining or making any point at all and had tried to play with the dog and make the best of it. I get it was their house and their pet but as well, I think it's good to consider guests, too rather than try and force a reaction out of me of sorts. I get anxious around dogs but I always try and be respectful towards peoples' pets, I just don't want to live with them myself and it's an issue with potential relationship matches that doesn't get enough airing.  Lonewolf made a good point about two people with pets needing to consider how their pets interact with one another.
